title: Monocyte - Definition and Examples - Biology Online Dictionary
abstract:
Monocytes are considered cells of first-line defense against pathogens. Monocytes engulf the attaching pathogen due to its phagocytic nature. The [plasma membrane](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/plasma-membrane) of monocytes helps to engulf the pathogen followed by its digestion or breakdown. Thus, monocytes function to remove dead cells, pathogens, dead or damaged cells, and [cancer cells](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/cancer). Under certain conditions like cancer cells and inflammatory diseases, monocytes are capable of either stimulating or inhibiting T-cells response. Also, monocytes have been found to play a role in neovascularization and tissue repair.  
All vertebrates have monocytes. By population, monocytes are 5% of the nucleated cells present in adult [blood](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/blood). Thus, monocytes are an integral part of the innate [immune system](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/immune-system) that also helps to maintain cellular homeostasis, especially during any inflammatory condition like an [infection](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/infection). The average half-life of monocytes is approximately 1 to 3 days.
**Overview:**
[Hematopoiesis](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/hematopoiesis) is the process of forming new blood cellular elements in vertebrates. It begins with a *multipotent stem cell*, a **hemocytoblast**, which gives rise to a common myeloid progenitor cell (CMP). The CMP, in turn, gives rise to granulocyte-monocyte colony-forming units (CFU-GM), also called *granulocyte-macrophage progenitor*. The CFU-GM may partially differentiate into CFU-G (a precursor in myelocyte-granulocyte series) or CFU-M (a precursor in the monocyte-macrophage series). The CFU-GM serves as the precursor for [monoblasts](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/monoblast) and [myeloblasts](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/myeloblast). In the **monocytic series**, the monoblast is a precursor cell for **promonocyte**. The promonocyte matures into a [monocyte](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/monocyte). The monocyte migrates from the [bone marrow](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/bone-marrow) to the peripheral blood through diapedesis. In humans, it constitutes 2% to 10% of the white blood cells in the body. In humans, some of the monocytes are stored in the spleen. As a type of [white blood cell](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/white-blood-cell) (leukocyte), the monocyte belongs to the [mononuclear leukocytes](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/mononuclear-leukocyte) as opposed to other white blood cells that are polymorphonuclear.
## Structure  
Monocytes are the largest of the white blood cell having a diameter of 12 to 20 µm (roughly estimated to be twice the size of [red blood cells](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/red-blood-cell) (RBCs)). Monocytes are mononuclear structures that have an ellipsoidal or kidney-shaped nucleus. Monocytes have a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio (approximately 3:1). Monocytes are amoeboid structures having non-granulated cytoplasm and are hence sometimes referred to as **agranulocytes**. Although, sometimes, monocytes contain small **azurophil granules** scattered in the pale blue [cytoplasm](https://www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/cytoplasm) (Figure 1).
